design_detail: Longitudinal observational study within a UCSD programme project on methamphetamine, HIV and HCV. 83 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence and 38 healthy comparison participants were tested at baseline and again after a mean 13 months (SD 5.6, range 6–42). Users were classified after the fact by self-reported methamphetamine use over the interval: Abstinent (no reported use, n=25) or Non-Abstinent (any reported use, n=58). Outcomes: demographically corrected T-scores for 7 cognitive domains and a global score, the Beck Depression Inventory and the Profile of Mood States. Only people with both visits are analysed.
can_establish: Whether, among people with methamphetamine dependence who came back for retesting, those who reported no use over about a year changed differently on neuropsychological and mood measures from those who reported use and from healthy comparison participants who were also retested.
cannot_establish: That stopping methamphetamine caused any change (abstinence was self-selected, self-reported only, and went together with less alcohol and cannabis use and unrecorded treatment), that the baseline differences from controls were caused by methamphetamine (no pre-use data; over half the users had HIV, and conditions excluded in controls were common in users), or that the larger gains of the 6 abstainers impaired at baseline exceed regression to the mean.

sample.recruitment: San Diego community and substance-use treatment programmes, for a NIDA-funded programme project at the University of California, San Diego (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph). The share recruited through treatment, and any treatment received during the interval, are not reported; the authors state they had no data on interval treatment (Discussion, last paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine group: SCID DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence in the lifetime and within 18 months of baseline; self-reported use within 90 days of baseline; at least 10 days' abstinence before testing, checked by urine toxicology. History of cannabis abuse or dependence allowed; past-12-month alcohol abuse allowed; lifetime alcohol dependence allowed if not met in the past 12 months; abuse or dependence on other substances in the past 12 months excluded (the sentence also mentions a 5-year window and is ambiguous). HIV and HCV infection allowed. Comparison group: methamphetamine-, HIV- and HCV-negative; excluded for antisocial personality disorder, ADHD or lifetime dependence on any substance. All participants: excluded for neurological conditions (seizures, closed head injury, stroke) and severe psychiatric conditions (schizophrenia, intellectual disability) (Method › Participants, paragraphs 1–3).
sample.demographics: Abstinent / Non-Abstinent / comparison (Table 1): age 36.2 (7.4) / 38.5 (7.6) / 35.4 (12.5) years; education 12.4 (2.8) / 12.7 (2.3) / 13.4 (1.7) years; men 88.0% / 91.4% / 81.6%; Caucasian 84.0% / 75.9% / 76.3% (all p>0.10). WRAT-3 reading 97.6 (12.1) / 99.3 (10.1) / 103.7 (9.4), omnibus p=0.075. HIV-positive 56% (n=14) / 59% (n=34) / 0; HCV 28% / 32% / 0. Lifetime bipolar disorder 20% (n=5) / 0 / 0 (p=0.002); antisocial personality disorder 20% / 19% / 0; lifetime ADHD 28% / 13.21% / 0; lifetime major depression 32.0% / 44.8% / 26.3%. Impaired at baseline (global deficit score above 0.5): 24% / 38% / 16% (p=0.049). Tobacco use not reported.
sample.attrition: Not reported. All 121 participants have both visits; how many were tested at baseline and did not return, and whether they differed from those who did, is not stated anywhere in the paper. Every analysis is of completers. Degrees of freedom imply 1 missing BDI and 2 missing POMS scores (F(1,117), F(1,116)); the cognitive F values in Tables 3–4 reproduce from the printed means and SDs with all 121 (editors' check).
sample.selection_effects: (1) Completers only: people who relapsed heavily or became unwell may be under-represented among those retested, and no comparison of returners with non-returners is given. (2) The Abstinent/Non-Abstinent split is self-selected and self-reported; abstainers had been abstinent longer at baseline (54.8 vs 40.2 days, p=0.033), had more bipolar disorder (20% vs 0%), and used less alcohol (36% vs 76%) and cannabis (32% vs 62%) during the interval (Table 2). (3) Comparison participants were screened free of HIV, HCV, antisocial personality disorder, ADHD and substance dependence, all common among users, so user–control differences combine methamphetamine with these conditions. (4) Mixed treatment and community recruitment in unknown proportions.

exposure.measurement: Lifetime and recent methamphetamine dependence by SCID (DSM-IV); age at first use, duration, quantity and recency from a detailed lifetime substance-use interview (self-report). Interval status from self-report at the follow-up psychiatric evaluation: any reported use placed a participant in the Non-Abstinent group. There was no biological check of use over the interval, which the authors list as a limitation (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Discussion, last paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Abstinent vs Non-Abstinent (Table 2): age at first use 24.5 (8.1) vs 25.4 (13.3); total duration of use 3167 (1975) vs 2787 (2070) days; lifetime quantity 3153 (3009) vs 2136 (2628) g; ever injected 48.0% vs 43.1% (all p>0.10). During the interval, 25% of the Non-Abstinent group met DSM-IV abuse and 54% DSM-IV dependence criteria for methamphetamine; the amount, frequency and timing of interval use were not recorded (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Discussion, last paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Common and unequal across groups (Table 2; Abstinent / Non-Abstinent / comparison). Lifetime dependence: alcohol 32.0% / 29.3% / 0; cannabis 16.0% / 19.0% / 0; cocaine 16.0% / 15.5% / 0. Past-12-month abuse: alcohol 36.0% / 37.9% / 15.8%; cannabis 24.0% / 32.8% / 15.8%. Lifetime alcohol and cannabis quantities far higher in both user groups than in controls. Any alcohol use during the interval 36% / 76% / 83%; any cannabis use 32% / 62% / 22%. The paper reports that cognitive change was not associated with lifetime alcohol, cocaine or other-substance abuse (all p>0.05, no statistics shown); interval alcohol and cannabis use were not entered in any reported model.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Baseline: at least 10 days, checked by urine toxicology; self-reported days since last use 54.8 (28.5) Abstinent vs 40.2 (20.1) Non-Abstinent. Follow-up: days since last use 378.8 (107.6) vs 68.8 (102.3), self-reported (Table 2). Whether urine toxicology was repeated at the follow-up visit is not stated; the paper mentions urine testing only for baseline.

comparison.controls: 38 healthy comparison participants (methamphetamine-, HIV- and HCV-negative; no antisocial personality disorder, ADHD or lifetime substance dependence; 6 met alcohol abuse and 6 cannabis abuse criteria in the past 12 months), retested at follow-up (Method › Participants, 3rd paragraph). The retest interval is reported for the whole sample only, not by group; how controls were recruited is not described separately.
comparison.matching: Not individually matched. Groups did not differ significantly in age, education, ethnicity or sex (Table 1). Cognitive scores are T-scores corrected for age, education, sex and ethnicity where indicated (Procedure).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use cognitive or mood data. Premorbid ability was estimated with WRAT-3 reading, which was lower in both user groups (97.6 and 99.3 vs 103.7; omnibus p=0.075; editors' pairwise standardized differences about 0.58 and 0.45, Student t p≈0.03 each, from Table 1) and was not adjusted for, although the text says the groups did not differ. ADHD and antisocial personality disorder were present in users and excluded in controls; school history, learning disorders and milder head injury are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Lifetime dependence on any substance excluded; past-12-month alcohol abuse 15.8% and cannabis abuse 15.8%; 83% drank alcohol and 22% used cannabis during the interval (Table 2). Tobacco use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Executive functions: Halstead Category Test, WCST-64, Trail Making B, Stroop interference. Learning: HVLT-R and BVMT-R total recall. Memory: HVLT-R and BVMT-R delayed recall. Motor: Grooved Pegboard (single test). Speed of information processing: WAIS-III Digit Symbol and Symbol Search, Trail Making A, Stroop colour. Verbal fluency: letter (FAS) and category (animals). Working memory: WAIS-III Letter-Number Sequencing, PASAT-50. Premorbid estimate: WRAT-3 reading. Mood: Beck Depression Inventory (1987 manual) and Profile of Mood States total score (Procedure).
outcomes.validity_norms: Raw scores converted to demographically corrected T-scores from published norms (mean 50, SD 10) and averaged into domain and global scores (Data Analyses, 1st paragraph). This gives a normative anchor: the user groups' baseline global means of 46.2–47.1 lie about 0.3–0.4 normative SD below the norm mean, and controls were at 50.1 (Table 3). Whether alternate test forms were used at retest is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Baseline impairment = global deficit score (mean of per-test deficit scores from 0, T above 40, to 5, T 19 or below) above 0.5, which the authors equate with roughly the 16th percentile (Data Analyses, 1st paragraph). Change = time × group and time × group × baseline-impairment interactions in repeated-measures ANOVA, followed by uncorrected paired and independent t-tests. The 'recovery' in the abstract rests on (a) the follow-up post hoc test of abstainers vs controls turning non-significant and (b) gains in the subgroup impaired at baseline.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Domain composites were used to limit comparisons (Data Analyses, 1st paragraph), but 8 cognitive outcomes were each tested in two interaction models, plus 2 mood outcomes, with follow-up t-tests at uncorrected p<0.05; the authors say they emphasized trends because samples were small (Discussion, last paragraph). The only significant three-way interaction (processing speed, p=0.014) would not survive a Bonferroni correction across the 8 cognitive outcomes (threshold about 0.006; editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Trained psychometrists followed manualized procedures; whether they knew participants' group or interval use is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Global T, baseline → follow-up (Tables 3–4): Abstinent 47.1 (5.1) → 50.1 (3.6), +3.0; Non-Abstinent 46.2 (6.1) → 47.8 (6.3), +1.6; controls 50.1 (5.2) → 52.8 (5.1), +2.7. Time F(1,118)=55.12, p<0.01; group × time F=2.11, p=0.126 (printed df 188). Editors' calculation (pooled SD): abstainers vs controls d≈0.58 at baseline and ≈0.59 at follow-up; Non-Abstinent vs controls ≈0.68 and ≈0.85. Within-group change d as reported: Abstinent 0.67, controls 0.52 (Discussion, 2nd and 5th paragraphs); the paper does not state the formula (editors reproduce 0.68 and 0.52 with mean change over the root-mean-square of the two SDs). Subgroups impaired at baseline (Table 5): abstainers n=6, global 41.26 → 47.94 (d=1.73, t=3.66, p=0.015); controls n=6, 43.70 → 47.01 (editors' d≈1.4–1.65 depending on denominator); Non-Abstinent n=22, 40.33 → 42.37. Three-way interaction: global F(2,115)=2.88, p=0.061; processing speed F(2,115)=4.45, p=0.014; motor F(2,115)=3.06, p=0.051; other domains p≥0.46. Processing speed in impaired abstainers 45.86 → 54.08 (reported d=0.69 in Results, 1.23 in Discussion; editors 1.26–1.35). Motor 44.33 → 54.00 (reported d=1.20 in Results, 1.09 in Discussion). Mood, editors' calculation (change over root-mean-square SD): BDI Abstinent 15.5 → 9.0 (d≈−0.75), Non-Abstinent 12.5 → 11.6 (−0.09), controls 3.4 → 4.5 (+0.21), time × group F(2,117)=8.71, p<0.001; POMS 79.1 → 55.3 (−0.59), 71.1 → 67.0 (−0.10), 38.2 → 43.3 (+0.16), F(2,116)=4.72, p=0.008. No confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.covariates: None in the primary models. HIV and HCV status were added as factors in post hoc repeated-measures models within the user groups and the results are described as unchanged (p values only). Associations of cognitive change with methamphetamine-use parameters and with lifetime alcohol, cocaine and other-substance abuse were tested and reported as non-significant without statistics (Results, 2nd paragraph). WRAT-3 reading, retest interval, interval alcohol and cannabis use, bipolar disorder and treatment were not adjusted for.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol mentioned. Moderation by baseline cognitive status is announced as an aim at the end of the Introduction; the domain-level three-way analyses are described as exploratory and the HIV/HCV analyses as post hoc (Data Analyses, paragraphs 2–3).
analysis.selective_reporting: Between-group Cohen's d values are announced in Data Analyses but not reported; effect sizes are given only for selected within-subgroup changes. The abstract reports the three-way interaction as observed although for the global score it was p=0.061, and presents the processing-speed result (one of 8 cognitive outcomes) without noting that the five other domains showed no such interaction (p≥0.46). The non-significant group × time interaction of the main model (p=0.126) is not in the abstract. Moderator analyses are reported only as non-significant, without statistics.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors acknowledge small samples (Discussion, last paragraph). The subgroups that carry the recovery claim have n=6 (abstainers impaired at baseline) and n=6 (controls impaired at baseline). Editors' approximation: with 25 vs 38 participants, power was about 48% to detect a standardized difference of 0.5 and about 21% for 0.3 (two-sided α=0.05); two subgroups of 6 had about 35% power for a difference of 1.0.

interpretation_gap.results_show: All groups improved on retest; abstainers' gain on the global score (+3.0 T) was close to that of retested controls (+2.7 T), and the main-model group × time interaction was not significant (p=0.126). The abstainer–control gap was 3.0 T at baseline and 2.7 T at follow-up (editors' d about 0.58 and 0.59). By domain, the gap narrowed for processing speed (2.8 → 0.2 T) and motor speed (5.5 → 3.5 T), was unchanged for learning, memory and fluency, and widened for executive functions (2.5 → 3.4 T) and working memory (3.3 → 5.0 T), where abstainers became significantly worse than controls only at follow-up. The 6 abstainers impaired at baseline gained 6.7 T, but the 6 controls impaired at baseline also gained 3.3 T, participants impaired at baseline gained more in every group (time × baseline-status p=0.006), and the three-way interaction for the global score was p=0.061. Depressive symptoms fell in abstainers (BDI 15.5 → 9.0) but remained above controls (4.5) at follow-up; POMS distress in abstainers was no longer different from controls.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that at follow-up abstainers and controls were comparable in global performance and in affective distress, that an interaction between baseline impairment, abstinence and improvement was observed, and that the results suggest "partial recovery of neuropsychological functioning" upon sustained abstinence (Abstract). The Discussion calls the study the first controlled longitudinal study of longer-term recovery and describes a further period of neuropsychological recovery over many months (Discussion, 1st paragraph); it argues that impaired abstainers improved beyond practice effects by comparing them with the whole control group (d 1.73 vs 0.52) rather than with the controls impaired at baseline (Discussion, 5th paragraph); and it speaks of the benefits of abstinence on mood (Discussion, 7th paragraph). The comparability claim rests on a post hoc test crossing p=0.05 while the gap barely changed, and the editors' recalculation under the stated t-test method gives p≈0.025 at follow-up (see reporting issues). Regression to the mean is not discussed anywhere. The BDI result contradicts the claim of comparable affective distress. The authors do call the findings preliminary and list self-reported abstinence and small samples as limitations (Discussion, 4th and last paragraphs).

timeline.event: Follow-up PET study: 5 users rescanned after a mean 14 months of abstinence; motor and memory tests repeated in those 5 users only, with non-significant trends (per the encyclopedia's first-pass card). Iudicello et al. cite it as showing cognitive improvement relative to controls, and label it with the wrong letter (see reporting issues).
Same programme: 5 users retested at 12–17 months, tests in users only; thalamic metabolic change correlated with change on some tests (per the encyclopedia's first-pass card).

Meta-analysis that, as summarized by Iudicello et al. (Introduction, 4th paragraph), found no association between length of abstinence and neuropsychological deficits; Iudicello et al. note that many included studies lacked abstinence data.

Simon et al. (2010): with urine-verified abstinence on a research ward, 18 users retested after about 25 days did not change significantly more than 21 retested controls (composite p=0.33; editors' d≈0.32, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96) (appraised in sc_simon_2010 from this reading batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Longitudinal evidence on cognitive change with sustained abstinence from methamphetamine remains thin. This study is one of the few with a retested control group, and its own tables show abstainers' overall change close to that of controls; the recovery signal is confined to small subgroups and to processing and motor speed, and has not been tested with biologically verified abstinence. The improvement in self-reported mood with abstinence is larger and more consistent than the cognitive change but is equally open to confounding by reduced alcohol and cannabis use, treatment and regression to the mean.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health / National Institute on Drug Abuse grant 5R01DA12065-08 (principal investigator Igor Grant); the HIV Neurobehavioral Research Center is supported by NIMH Center award MH 62512 (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the PMC author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: HIV Neurobehavioral Research Center, affiliated with UC San Diego, the Naval Hospital San Diego and the VA San Diego Healthcare System; the paper carries a disclaimer that the views are not those of the Navy, the Department of Defense or the US Government. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study that retests people with methamphetamine use disorder and matched non-using comparison participants at identical intervals with alternate forms, verifies abstinence biologically throughout, reports who was lost to follow-up, and analyses change with methods that remove regression to the mean (impairment defined on a separate baseline test, or follow-up adjusted for baseline), with pre-registered hypotheses and subgroups large enough to test them.

domains.note: Abstinence over the interval was self-selected and went with less interval alcohol and cannabis use, longer baseline abstinence and more bipolar disorder; treatment unknown; none adjusted. User–control contrasts confounded by HIV (over half of users), HCV, ADHD, antisocial personality disorder and lower WRAT-3 reading.
Interval abstinence by self-report only, with no biological verification; the Non-Abstinent group combines a single reported use with renewed dependence.

Analysis restricted to people who returned for follow-up (selection on a post-baseline event); groups defined by post-baseline behaviour; mixed treatment and community recruitment in unknown proportions.
Treatment during the interval not recorded; retest interval ranged from 6 to 42 months and is not reported by group.
Number of baseline participants not retested, and their characteristics, are not reported.
Standardized, normed tests and a retested control group, but assessor blinding and alternate forms not reported; mood outcomes are self-report by participants who knew their own abstinence status.

Ten outcomes in several models without correction; the abstract foregrounds the single significant three-way interaction and a non-significant post hoc test; promised between-group effect sizes not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High risk in five domains, several of which favour finding recovery in the abstinent group (uncontrolled differences in interval alcohol and cannabis use, regression to the mean in subgroups selected for low baseline scores, emphasis on the one significant interaction among ten outcomes). Under ROBINS-E, multiple high-risk domains that substantially lower confidence justify very high overall for the abstinence-related change estimates. The baseline user–control differences are better measured but remain confounded (high).

key_findings.finding: 121 participants with both visits were analysed: 83 with methamphetamine dependence (25 reporting no use over the interval, 58 reporting any use) and 38 controls; mean retest interval 13 months (SD 5.6, range 6–42). Attrition from baseline is not reported.
Interval abstinence was classified by self-report at the follow-up psychiatric evaluation; urine toxicology is mentioned only for confirming at least 10 days' abstinence before the baseline visit.
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Discussion, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline global T: Abstinent 47.1 (5.1), Non-Abstinent 46.2 (6.1), controls 50.1 (5.2); F=5.70, p=0.004; both user groups below controls and not different from each other. Editors' d vs controls about 0.58 and 0.68.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 1st and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: At baseline 24% of abstainers, 38% of the Non-Abstinent group and 16% of controls were classified as impaired (global deficit score above 0.5; overall p=0.049; only Non-Abstinent differed from controls). About 34% of the 83 users were impaired.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Method › Participants, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: All groups improved on retest (time F(1,118)=55.12, p<0.01); the group × time interaction for the global score was not significant (F=2.11, p=0.126).
key_findings.note: Printed as F(2,188); the error df should be 118 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Follow-up global T: Abstinent 50.1 (3.6), Non-Abstinent 47.8 (6.3), controls 52.8 (5.1); F=9.59, p<0.001; post hoc, only the Non-Abstinent group differed from controls. Change from baseline: +3.0, +1.6 and +2.7 T; the abstainer–control gap went from 3.0 to 2.7 T.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' recalculation from Table 4 (Student t, 25 vs 38) gives p≈0.025 for abstainers vs controls at follow-up, not p>0.05; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: At follow-up abstainers scored significantly below controls on executive functions (50.9 vs 54.3) and working memory (48.4 vs 53.4), domains where they had not differed at baseline; the processing-speed gap closed (52.6 vs 52.8).
key_findings.locator: Tables 3–4; Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within-group global change was reported as d=0.67 for abstainers, against a mean d=0.38 for the Non-Abstinent group and controls combined; the controls' own retest change was d=0.52.

Six abstainers impaired at baseline improved from 41.26 to 47.94 global T (d=1.73, t=3.66, p=0.015); six controls impaired at baseline improved from 43.70 to 47.01 and 22 impaired Non-Abstinent users from 40.33 to 42.37. The time × group × baseline-impairment interaction was p=0.061; the time × baseline-impairment interaction was p=0.006.
key_findings.locator: Table 5; Figure 1 (image); Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Impaired participants improved more in every group, the pattern expected from regression to the mean (editors' interpretation; not discussed in the paper).

key_findings.finding: Processing speed showed a significant three-way interaction (F(2,115)=4.45, p=0.014): impaired abstainers (n=6) rose from 45.86 to 54.08 T (t=3.80, p=0.013); controls impaired at baseline fell from 47.50 to 46.08.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 3rd paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: Effect size reported as d=0.69 (Results) and d=1.23 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); Table 5 gives 1.26–1.35 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Motor speed (Grooved Pegboard only) showed a trend-level three-way interaction (F(2,115)=3.06, p=0.051): impaired abstainers (n=6) rose from 44.33 to 54.00 T (t=3.08, p=0.028, d=1.20).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 3rd paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: Discussion, 3rd paragraph, gives d=1.09 for the same change.

key_findings.finding: Cognitive change in the user groups was reported as unrelated to age at first use, recency, cumulative duration and quantity of methamphetamine use, HIV and HCV status, and lifetime alcohol, cocaine and other-substance abuse (all p>0.05; no statistics shown).

BDI: time × group F(2,117)=8.71, p<0.001. Abstainers 15.5 (9.9) → 9.0 (7.1) (paired t=−3.79, p<0.001); Non-Abstinent 12.5 → 11.6 and controls 3.4 → 4.5 did not change significantly. Both user groups had higher BDI than controls at baseline and at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mood Symptoms and Affective Distress, 1st paragraph; Tables 3–4; Figure 2 (image)

key_findings.finding: POMS total: time × group F(2,116)=4.72, p=0.008. Abstainers 79.1 → 55.3 (t=3.71, p=0.001); Non-Abstinent 71.1 → 67.0 and controls 38.2 → 43.3 not significant. At follow-up only the Non-Abstinent group exceeded controls. Within abstainers, mood improvement was not correlated with cognitive improvement (p>0.10).
key_findings.locator: Results › Mood Symptoms and Affective Distress, 2nd paragraph; Tables 3–4; Figure 3 (image)

key_findings.finding: During the interval, any alcohol use was reported by 36% of abstainers, 76% of the Non-Abstinent group and 83% of controls; any cannabis use by 32%, 62% and 22%.
Over half of each user group was HIV-positive (56% and 59%) and 28–32% had HCV; controls were selected to have neither.

reporting_issues.issue: The group × time interaction is printed as F(2,188) = 2.11; with 121 participants in 3 groups the error df is 118, as printed for the time effect F(1,118). The printed p=0.126 matches df 118 (editors' check).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The text and Table 4 report abstainers as no longer different from controls on the global score at follow-up (p>0.05), and the footnote to Table 4 says post hoc comparisons were independent-samples t-tests. From the means and SDs in Table 4 (50.1 (3.6), n=25 vs 52.8 (5.1), n=38) a Student t-test gives t≈2.29, df=61, p≈0.025 (Welch p≈0.017); only with the three-group pooled error term (Fisher LSD) is p≈0.058. The baseline comparison reported as significant gives p≈0.028 (Student) or 0.041 (LSD). Editors' calculations; the one-way F values in Tables 3–4 all reproduce from the same means and SDs.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 4 and footnote a; Results › Global Cognitive Functioning, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline claim that abstainers became comparable to controls is not reproducible under the stated method; at best it rests on a p-value moving from about 0.04 to about 0.06 while the gap changed from 3.0 to 2.7 T-points.

reporting_issues.issue: The processing-speed effect size for impaired abstainers is given as d=0.69 (Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph) and as d=1.23 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); Table 5 gives 1.26 (baseline SD) to 1.35 (root-mean-square SD) by editors' calculation. The comparison subgroups' mean is 0.12 in the Results and 0.16 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: The magnitude of the paper's one significant domain-level finding is reported inconsistently; the table supports the larger value, but n=6.

reporting_issues.issue: The motor effect size for impaired abstainers is given as d=1.20 (Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph) and d=1.09 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the editors reproduce 1.20 with the root-mean-square SD.

reporting_issues.issue: For the global score, the remaining subgroups' change is given as mean d=0.60, range 0.31 to 1.27. From Table 5 the six controls impaired at baseline changed by 3.31 T, d≈1.39 (root-mean-square SD) or 1.65 (baseline SD), above the stated maximum. The paper also uses different denominators for different d values (1.73 reproduces with the baseline SD, 0.67 and 1.20 with the root-mean-square SD) without stating the formula.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates how much the impaired control subgroup also improved, which is the comparator for regression to the mean.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says abstainers and controls had comparable affective distress at follow-up, but the Results and Table 4 show both user groups with higher BDI scores than controls at follow-up (p<0.05); only POMS distress was no longer different.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Mood Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Table 4
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates normalization of mood.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that an interaction between baseline impairment, abstinence and improvement was observed; for the global score it was p=0.061, significant only for processing speed (p=0.014) among 8 cognitive outcomes, with motor p=0.051.
reporting_issues.consequence: A trend and one uncorrected significant result are presented as an observed interaction.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that cognitive change and mood change were unrelated to alcohol and cannabis use during the interval (2nd and 7th paragraphs); the Results report only tests against lifetime alcohol, cocaine and other-substance abuse diagnoses and show no analysis of interval alcohol or cannabis use.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd and 7th paragraphs; Results › 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A key confounder (abstainers drank and used cannabis far less over the interval) is dismissed by an analysis that is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: Signs of paired t statistics are inconsistent: for POMS, the abstainers' decrease is reported as t=3.71 and the Non-Abstinent group's decrease as t=−0.84; for BDI, the abstainers' decrease is t=−3.79.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Mood Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; direction must be read from Tables 3–4.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: lifetime ADHD in the Non-Abstinent group is printed as 13.21% (n=7), which is 7/53, not 7/58 (12.07%), implying 5 unreported missing values; HCV 32% cannot be obtained from 58 participants (18/58 = 31.0%, 19/58 = 32.8%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; undisclosed missing data on a psychiatric covariate.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2: lifetime dependence on other substances in the Abstinent group is printed as 4.0% (n=4); 4 of 25 is 16%, and 4.0% is 1 of 25.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one of the two values is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the groups did not differ in estimated premorbid intelligence (p>0.05); the omnibus WRAT-3 test was p=0.075 and pairwise differences between each user group and controls are about 0.45–0.58 SD (editors' calculation, Student t p≈0.03 each).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Method › Participants, 4th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: A premorbid difference of similar size to the baseline cognitive difference (d≈0.58–0.68) is not acknowledged or adjusted.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction cites 'Volkow et al., 2001b' for cognitive improvement after nine months of abstinence, but the paper's reference list assigns 2001b to the American Journal of Psychiatry cross-sectional study (encyclopedia volkow_2001a); the follow-up study is the Journal of Neuroscience paper (their 2001a; encyclopedia volkow_2001b). The Introduction also describes that improvement and the one after 17 months (Wang et al., 2004) as relative to healthy comparison participants, whereas the encyclopedia's first-pass cards record tests in 5 users only.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-references must use the J Neurosci paper; the prior-literature summary overstates those studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The retest interval is reported only for the whole sample (13 months). For abstainers, days since last use rose from 54.8 to 378.8, which implies a mean interval of about 324 days (10.7 months) if they truly did not use (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Practice-effect comparisons with controls assume similar intervals, which cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The T-score to deficit-score conversion as printed assigns 0 to T above 40 and 1 to T 35–39, leaving T=40 unassigned.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; presumably T 40 or above scores 0.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4 the Abstinent group's Learning and Memory T-scores at follow-up are identical (48.1, SD 8.6), while the other two groups differ between the two domains; one of the two rows may be a copy error.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstainers' follow-up learning and memory values cannot both be relied on; no claim should rest on either until the source is checked.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2911490 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1–5 as text; Figures 1–3 are images, legends read, values taken from the tables; no supplementary files)

editorial_corrections.to: reporting issue added: identical Learning and Memory values for abstainers in Table 4
editorial_corrections.reason: Found by the editor while checking Table 4 during review round 1 source checks (saved PubMed Central page text).
